text.p: Furniture and electrical goods retailer Harvey Norman Holdings Ltd said after releasing its full year sales results on Friday that it expected a better profit in the year to June 30, 1997 than in 1995/96.

"We're expecting it to be better than last year," Harvey Norman Managing Director Michael Harvey told Reuters in an interview. He said the retail climate appeared to strengthen substantially in recent months to its best levels in almost two years as consumers warmed to recent interest rate cuts.

Earlier, Harvey Norman released sales figures for the year to June 30 showing total sales from Harvey Norman's franchised stores and its own store rose 16.7 percent to A$1.216 billion, bettering Harvey Norman's target of a 15 percent rise.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's three rate cuts in the second half of 1996 appeared not to have had much effect initially as consumers repaid debt before spending on consumer items like televisions, computers and furniture, Harvey said.
But the Reserve Bank's surprise 50 basis point cut in May this year appeared to have convinced consumers that rates would stay low and had sparked a surge in consumption, he said.
"It came through pretty strongly in June which really gave us the extra boost we needed to get over the line," Harvey said, referring to the group's A$1.2 billion annual sales target.
"It's looking good. Everybody is looking forward to a strong half and it's probably the most positive news we've had for the last couple of years," he said.

Retailing had been tough since a slowdown in November 1995 sparked by speculation of an early election, followed by the actual election in March 1996 and sluggishness through the rest of 1996 and into early 1997, Harvey said.
"The first few interest rate cuts didn't really kick in and there's a wide feeling that the last one has been the one to help make people's mind up," he said.
"There's definitely been pent up demand over the last 18 months to two years and it looks like people are now dipping in and saying let's have a spend," he said.

Harvey said the recovery had been strongest in the group's furniture lines, which had seen sales growth for the year of about 20 percent. Electronic goods sales growth had been dragged back by a competitive television, video and audio sector to about 15 percent on the year.

Computer sales growth had been about 13 percent for the year, but this was expected to accelerate in the coming year as Harvey Norman expanded distribution of its cut-rate Harvey Norman-brand computer and as the government cracked down on competitors who were not charging sales tax.

The strong performance of the furniture sector was a good sign for the group as it was the most established sector, he said. "It certainly feels good and the feedback from the stores is as positive as we've seen since that dreaded November 1995."

He said Harvey Norman planned to continue its expansion, opening another six new stores through the rest of calendar 1997, including one more in New Zealand. That would take Harvey Norman's total number of stores to 65.

Harvey said he could not be any more specific about how much higher the 1996/97 profit would be than the A$30.41 million profit posted in 1995/96, except to say that the outlook was good. Harvey Norman shares were down nine cents at A$7.55 at 2.30 a.m. (0430 GMT).
